bullets.text: The purpose of the meeting was to discuss various Talk page workflows, user onboarding experiences, and editor interaction tools before breaking into small working groups.
Welcome messages are most effective when kept simple and signed by an active user who can promptly answer questions, rather than using complex boilerplate templates.
Editors handling vandal warnings and reversions need more targeted notification options so they only receive alerts when a user provides a substantive reply.
Workflows often stem from passively monitoring other user Talk pages or using the New Pages feed to discover articles needing collaborative improvements or translations.
There is a desire to expand acknowledgment features like Thanks, WikiLove, and Barnstars, as well as replace Edward's Bot for project newsletters and invitations.

The group discussed how users perceive welcome messages, noting that tests show editors often cannot distinguish between automated bots and real humans unless messages are kept simple and conversational.
Speaker A shared personal experiences on the value of early human connections and mobilizing a global network of editors to collaborate on complex article topics.
Speaker D detailed the workflow of reverting vandalism, noting that automated watchlists create noise when editors only want notifications if a user provides a thoughtful response.
Participants analyzed passive Talk page monitoring, where editors discover and improve articles simply by observing conversations on other editors' pages.
Jake proposed enhancements to recognition tools such as the Thanks feature, Barn-O-Meters, and Barnstars, and called for an improved alternative to Edward's Bot for bulk notifications.
Speaker F described utilizing the New Pages feed to find newly created articles, locate relevant sources, and coordinate with original creators on translations.
The facilitator will read through the summarized list of discussed workflows shown on the board.
Attendees will divide into small breakout groups to select and examine specific workflows.
The participants are experienced wiki editors and contributors discussing editor onboarding, community collaboration, and talk page communications.
The community has deployed and tested several tools to manage interactions, including automated welcome bots, Twinkle for reversions, and the New Pages feed.
Welcome messages often feel devoid of social cues, leaving new editors unable to tell if they are interacting with a human or a bot.
Editors performing manual reversions and leaving warning templates must watch entire talk pages to catch genuine replies, flooding their watchlists with unwanted notifications.
Global outreach tools like Edward's Bot are low-tech, difficult to use, and widely perceived by the community as spam.
Recognition mechanisms like Barnstars and thanks lack intuitive workflows for aggregating acknowledgments or sending quick reciprocal thank-yous.
Budget, authority, and timeline were not discussed.
Participants raised concerns that automated welcome templates feel impersonal and overwhelming compared to authentic human connections.
Speaker D objected to automatic talk page watchlisting, noting that it produces an unmanageable stream of notifications for unrelated user activities.
Mariana will summarize the discussed workflow topics on the board for the group.
Participants will divide into small breakout groups to select specific editor workflows and analyze them in detail.
Speaker E is continuing development work on an initiative to replace Edward's Bot.
Guide and welcome both new and experienced editors into the community through effective onboarding interactions.
Facilitate organic collaboration and content handoffs across international contributors on specialized topics.
Manage manual reversions and warning notices efficiently without cluttering editor watchlists.
Express gratitude and acknowledge editor contributions more easily through positive reinforcement mechanisms.
Wikidata's simplified automated welcome messages signed by recently active users have successfully initiated positive communication with newcomers.
Direct collaborative outreach enabled an article initiated in Japan to be rapidly expanded and translated across multiple regions.
The New Pages feed tool has proven useful for identifying new articles, adding sources, and coordinating translations with original authors.
Impersonal or overly complex welcome templates create confusion and lack social cues, making new users uncertain if they are interacting with humans or bots.
Editors tracking manual reversions risk overwhelming their watchlists with unwanted page updates when they only care about direct replies.
Community outreach and newsletters rely on Edward's Bot, which is perceived as a spam bot and a difficult, low-tech messaging mechanism.
Provide clear indications on whether welcome messages are automated while including interest-based starting recommendations.
Implement thread-level notifications on user talk pages so editors receive alerts only when a thoughtful reply is posted.
Enhance acknowledgment features by adding thank counters, easier display tools for Barnstars, and thank buttons on received awards.
Develop a modern replacement for Edward's Bot to support global messaging for newsletters, real-life events, and project notices.
Mariana will read aloud a summary of the discussed workflows recorded on the board.
Participants will split into small groups to each focus on a selected workflow.
Speaker A shared early editing experiences involving a personal welcome from user Polly Frog and a collaborative workflow coordinating editors across multiple countries on a math article.
Speaker G described Wikidata's automated welcome bot workflow, which delivers simple greetings signed by recently active users to open communication channels.
Speaker D detailed workflows for manual vandalism reversions using templated talk page warnings, as well as tracking other users' talk pages via watchlists to find editing tasks.
Jake outlined recognition workflows including Thanks, WikiLove, Barnstars, and the Barn-O-Meter, alongside mass participation messages like newsletters and Geo notices.
Speaker F described using the New Pages feed to monitor new articles, find sources, and reach out to page creators for translations.
Speaker B asked what kind of workflow could address confusion about welcome messages, and Speaker C suggested clearly indicating whether a message is automated or from a real person.
Speaker C asked where thoughtful responses to revert notices typically occur, and Speaker D answered that they happen on the other user's talk page.
Speaker E and Jake asked how Speaker D tracks replies without watching entire talk pages, prompting Speaker C to point out that the response-to-threads feature resolves this issue.
Speaker A asked for clarification on what EdwardsBot is, and Speaker D and Jake explained it is a low-tech global messaging bot used to send newsletters and event announcements.
Speaker C noted that initial welcome messages felt alien and confusing due to a lack of social cues about whether they came from a human or an automated bot.
Speaker E and Speaker F pointed out that user tests show an even 50/50 split in distinguishing human from bot welcomes, with Speaker E favoring fully automated onboarding messages.
Speaker B reflected that a simple, direct welcome message from Speaker G made them feel valued and at home upon joining.
Jake advocated for enhanced acknowledgment features, including a thank counter and interactive thanks buttons on Barnstars.
Speaker F praised the New Pages feed as an effective replacement for the previous new pages tool for monitoring and improving articles.
Speaker C and Speaker E agreed to return to the response-to-threads feature and talk page watchlisting later in the session.
Speaker E noted that development work is currently underway to replace EdwardsBot for mass messaging.
Speaker B arranged for the group to review the summarized workflows on the board and split into small breakout groups to examine individual workflows.

Q: Speaker B asked what kind of workflow could address the lack of social cues in talk page welcomes. — A: Speaker C suggested providing a clear indication of whether a welcome message is automated or from a real person.
Q: Speaker C asked where a thoughtful response from an editor actually occurs during a manual reversion workflow. — A: Speaker D clarified that the reply occurs on that user's talk page.

Q: Speaker E asked how Speaker D knows when a reverted editor responds to a warning message. — A: Speaker D stated they do not know, explaining they avoid keeping a watchlist that updates all day long.

Q: Speaker A asked what Edward's Bot is. — A: Jake and Speaker D explained that it is a global messaging tool, often called a spam bot, used to deliver mass notices like newsletters and event invitations.
Speaker C wondered early in their editing experience whether the welcome message left on their talk page originated from an automated bot or a real contributor.
Speaker D raised the question of how an editor can be alerted strictly to a thoughtful reply after issuing a warning, without watchlisting the entire user talk page and receiving unwanted updates.
Speaker C: "I think I did go to that person's top page and thank them, but it was like devoid of a lot of social cues that I think really makes the whole place kind of alien."
Speaker A: "The content was not what I contributed to that article. It was more the collaboration and connection."
Speaker D: "The thing is, I don't want to have a watch list that just goes on right freaking day."
Jake: "I would like it to be easier to give and thank and have those interactions where gratitude is expressed."

Speaker A shared positive experiences where personalized outreach from editor Polly Frog and cross-border collaboration across Japan, California, the UK, and Gaza fostered editor engagement and community connection.
Speaker G highlighted that Wikidata successfully opened communication with new editors by using simple welcome messages signed by recently active users who actively answer questions.
Speaker F found the New Pages feed tool highly effective for discovering new articles to improve and collaborating with original authors on translations.
Speaker C noted that initial welcome messages felt alienating and lacked social cues to distinguish whether they came from real users or automated bots.
Speaker F and Speaker E stated that user testing showed editors could only tell whether a welcome message was human or automated half of the time.
Speaker D reported that leaving templated warning messages on talk pages after manual reversions results in an overcrowded watchlist with irrelevant notifications.
Jake noted that Edward's Bot, used for delivering newsletters and community notices, is low-tech, difficult to operate, and widely regarded as spam.
Speaker E proposed making automated welcome messages explicit and customizing them with starter recommendations based on user interests.
Speaker G suggested keeping welcome greetings short and simple rather than overloading new editors with complex templates and links.
Speaker D and Speaker C supported thread response features so editors only receive notifications when an editor directly replies to a warning rather than watching an entire talk page.
Jake proposed enhancing appreciation features by adding a thank counter, placing thank buttons on Barnstars, and making it easier to collect and display badges.
Speaker E is working on a replacement for Edward's Bot to handle global and group messaging.
Mariana (Speaker A) was asked to read and summarize the discussed workflows on the board before the group splits into breakout sessions.
